items.stem: Why must a stem-and-leaf diagram include a key?
options: to show how the stems and leaves combine to give the values
items.answer: to show how the stems and leaves combine to give the values
items.markingKey: Without a key 3 | 5 could mean 35, 3.5 or 350.

items.stem: Explain why a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram is useful for comparing two data sets.
items.answer: Both sets share the same stems, so their shapes, centres and spreads can be compared directly side by side while keeping all values.
items.markingKey: B1 common stems; B1 compare shape/centre/spread directly [2]

items.stem: Explain why a stem-and-leaf diagram is not suitable for a data set of 500 values.
items.answer: There would be far too many leaves on each stem, making it hard to draw and read; a grouped table or histogram is better.
items.markingKey: B1 too many leaves; B1 alternative representation [2]

items.stem: In a histogram with unequal class widths, the height of each bar represents
items.answer: frequency density
items.markingKey: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

items.stem: Explain why frequency density, rather than frequency, is plotted when class widths are unequal.
items.answer: Wide classes would otherwise look too important; using frequency density makes the area of each bar proportional to its frequency.
items.markingKey: B1 wide classes exaggerated; B1 area ∝ frequency [2]

items.stem: Explain why there are no gaps between the bars of a histogram.
items.answer: The data are continuous and the classes are adjacent, so each class boundary is shared by neighbouring bars.
items.markingKey: B1 continuous data; B1 adjacent class boundaries [2]

items.answer: the area of its bar

Noah draws a histogram of the data 150 ≤ x < 155: 26; 155 ≤ x < 165: 12; 165 ≤ x < 180: 40; 180 ≤ x < 200: 96; 200 ≤ x < 230: 18 using the frequencies as the bar heights. Explain why the bar for 200 ≤ x < 230 is misleading and state the correct height.

items.stem: On a cumulative frequency graph, points are plotted at
items.answer: the upper class boundaries
items.markingKey: Cumulative frequency counts values up to the end of each class.

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a box-and-whisker plot compared with a histogram.
items.answer: Advantage: it shows the median, quartiles and outliers clearly and is easy to compare between groups. Disadvantage: it hides the detailed shape of the distribution (e.g. two peaks).
items.markingKey: B1 valid advantage; B1 valid disadvantage [2]

items.stem: Explain why the median read from a cumulative frequency graph of grouped data is an estimate.
items.answer: The raw values are unknown; the graph assumes values are spread evenly within each class (straight lines or a smooth curve between points).
items.markingKey: B1 raw data unknown; B1 assumption of even spread [2]
